### D27: Launch through LaunchServices; never touch CoreMotion in simulator mode (2026-11-07)
**Decision:** Always start the app with `open build/LouVoice.app` (or Finder), never by running the binary directly. Create `CMHeadphoneMotionManager` lazily, only when the AirPods source is selected. `--smoke` and `LOUVOICE_SOURCE=simulator` start on the simulator from `init`.
**Why:** The first smoke run was killed with `__TCC_CRASHING_DUE_TO_PRIVACY_VIOLATION__` inside CoreMotion. Run directly from a terminal, macOS holds the *parent* process responsible for the Motion permission. That parent has no `NSMotionUsageDescription`, so the system aborts the app. Launched with `open`, LouVoice itself is responsible and its Info.plist applies. Separately, the hub had been creating and stopping the motion manager even in simulator mode, which needlessly triggered the permission check.
**Consequence:** Smoke command: `open -W -n --env LOUVOICE_DATA_DIR=… build/LouVoice.app --args --smoke`.
EOF

content.text:
I built the native macOS app your updated PLAN.md describes. Everything runs on the simulator, but it hasn't touched real AirPods yet. Whether silent mouthing actually works is the next step, and it needs you wearing them.

**What I verified:**
- **Core checks:** all 9 pass (`swift run LouVoiceCheck`). They cover the even time grid, the drift filter, the re-seat correction, the matching, the classifier, an evaluation that only beats chance when there's real signal, and nod/shake detection.
- **Full app flow:** a `--smoke` run drives the app's real code on the simulator:
  - Enrollment ran 2 blocks with a re-seat break between them: 20 takes, none re-taken.
  - Evaluation, holding out whole blocks: 90% overall and 100% on words.
  - Decoding got 6 of 6 words right, each confirmed by a simulated nod and added back as training data.
- **Simulator caveats:** the numbers only show the app works end to end, not that AirPods do. Rejecting non-word movement scored 50%, from just 4 takes, far too few to judge. On all 8 default words the simulator scores 72% on words, because it makes "no", "stop" and "open" look almost identical.

**What I couldn't check:** how the screens look. This session has no Screen Recording permission, so I couldn't take a screenshot.

**Three things building it changed** (each logged in [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md)):
- **Trimming was broken (D22).** Each word sat at a random spot in its recording window, so matching failed half the time. Smoothing fixed it: one simulated check went from 12/24 to 24/24.
- **macOS can't tell which earbud is reporting (D21).** That API exists only on iOS, so takes record "unknown".
- **Always launch with `open` or Finder (D27).** Run straight from a terminal, macOS killed the app for a Motion-permission violation. Simulator mode now never touches the motion system at all.

**To prove the product works**, run:

```bash
scripts/build-app.sh && open build/LouVoice.app
```

1. Allow Motion when asked.
2. On **Sensors**, check it streams at about 25 Hz.
3. Run **Enroll**: 3 blocks, re-seating the AirPods between blocks, about 10 minutes.
4. Read the leave-one-block-out number on **Evaluate**. That number is the proof; the goal is 90% or better on 8 words.
5. If two words keep getting confused, swap one out and enroll again.

Nothing is committed yet; say the word and I'll commit and push. The stem-press trigger is still untested; Space always works. The logic is in `Sources/LouVoiceCore`, the app in `Sources/LouVoice`, and [README.md](README.md) has the commands.

**Decision:** The default vocabulary is the five words `hello, can, you, hear, me`. Each is enrolled and decoded on its own; the demo phrase is built by decoding the words one after another into the transcript.

content.text:
The app now trains on **hello, can, you, hear, me**. Each word is trained and recognised on its own, so you mouth the phrase one word per beep and the transcript builds up "hello can you hear me". The app is rebuilt and all 9 checks still pass. The change is logged as D28 in [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md), and [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) shows the new list.

**Expect trouble with the short words.** Four of the five are one syllable with little jaw movement. On the simulator, "hello" scores 100%, but "can" and "you" score only 56%, mostly mixed up with each other and with "me". Real jaw motion will probably show the same pattern. If it does, fix it in this order:
1. Exaggerate the jaw even more on "can", "you" and "me".
2. Record extra takes of whichever pair the Evaluate screen says is most confused.
3. For the demo, limit the active words to the expected next one or two using the context checklist on the Decode screen. Since the phrase order is fixed, this keeps accuracy high.

**To train it:**

```bash
open build/LouVoice.app
```

1. Allow Motion when asked, and confirm Sensors shows about 25 Hz.
2. On **Enroll**, run 3 blocks × 3 reps, re-seating the AirPods between blocks. That takes about 6 minutes.
3. On **Evaluate**, read the leave-one-block-out number. That's the honest result.
4. On **Decode**, press Space and mouth each word in turn, nodding to confirm each one.

.build/release/LouVoiceCheck | tail -1 && cat >> DECISIONS.md <<'EOF'

### D29: Every pipeline variable is tunable, with auto-tune on real takes (2026-11-07)
**Decision:** The feature and recognizer settings are collected into one `PipelineConfig`, persisted in UserDefaults. A new **Tune** screen exposes each one:
- sample rate and high-pass cutoff
- re-seat correction on/off and channel groups
- trim on/off, trim threshold, smoothing and padding
- k, augmented copies, augment rotation and time-warp, DTW band
- capture window and pre-roll

Changing a setting re-extracts features from the stored raw samples and retrains, so it takes effect on existing data immediately. **Auto-tune** is a greedy coordinate search: each variable in turn, scored by leave-one-block-out on your takes, keeping the best, two passes. `LouVoiceCheck --eval <dataset.json> [--tune]` does the same from the command line.
**Why:** The first real session scored 49% on held-out blocks. Fixed defaults chosen from the simulator were never going to be right for real jaw motion. Raw samples are stored, so every setting can be re-tested on recorded data without re-recording.
**Caveat:** Picking the best of about 60 trials on the same 59 takes is optimistic. With about 9 takes per word, one take moves a word's score by about 11 points, so differences under about 5 points are noise. Confirm with quiz takes (D31).

### D30: New defaults from the first real session (2026-11-07). *Amends D6 and D8.*
**Decision:** Resample at 25 Hz with the high-pass at **1.6 Hz** (was 0.8 Hz), and **8** augmented copies (was 4). Everything else unchanged.
**Evidence** (59 real takes, 3 blocks plus 2 confirmed decodes, leave-one-block-out):

| Settings | Accuracy | Words | Non-word rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original (0.8 Hz, ×4) | 49% | 51% | 42% |
| New defaults | 68% | 66% | 75% |

Chance is 20%, and p = 0.005 in both cases, so the motion carries real word information.
**Why these, not the auto-tune winner as-is:** The two top settings found (1.2 Hz with trim 45% and k=2, at 66%, and 1.6 Hz with trim 25% and aug ×8, at 68%) are within noise of each other. The consistent signal was "high-pass well above 0.8 Hz". The chosen default changes the fewest variables from the original, which overfits least.
**Also measured:** The AirPods deliver **50 Hz** on macOS (20 ms between samples), not the 25 Hz subvox reported. Resampling at 50 Hz scored the same or slightly worse and costs 4× more DTW, so 25 Hz stays.
**Reading:** A higher cutoff means the useful information is in fast jaw motion (above about 1.5 Hz). Slower head and posture movement was drowning it.

### D31: Continuous accuracy testing during training (2026-11-07)
**Decision:**
- **Test-then-train:** during enrollment, each take passes the quality gate and is then **predicted before it's saved**, by a model trained only on *other* blocks. The Enroll screen shows live accuracy: overall, per word, last 10 and by block.
- **Quiz rounds:** optional, on by default, after each block: one take per word, predicted by the model trained on everything so far, saved with `isTest = true` and **never trained on**. There is also a standalone quiz.
- Evaluate reports the held-out quiz accuracy next to leave-one-block-out, and can promote quiz takes into training once read.

**Why:** Accuracy was only visible after the fact. Testing every take as it comes in shows immediately which words fail and whether more blocks are helping. Quiz takes are the only number untouched by tuning (D29), because they are never trained on or tuned against.
**Consequence:** Block 1 of a first session has no live score (nothing to test against yet). Quiz rounds add about 25% to session time.

content.text:
I measured your 59 recorded takes honestly: each enrollment block is held out and predicted by a model trained on the other blocks. At the original settings they scored **49%**, against 20% for random guessing. The p-value of 0.005 means the AirPods motion really does carry word information. The signal was there; the settings were burying it.

**Tuning on your data took it to 68%:**

| | Overall | Words only | Not-a-word rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Original settings | 49% | 51% | 42% |
| New defaults | **68%** | 66% | 75% |

- **High-pass filter 1.6 Hz (was 0.8 Hz).** The useful jaw motion is fast; slower head movement was swamping it. This made most of the difference.
- **8 extra copies per take (was 4).** Each recorded take now gets 8 slightly varied copies for training instead of 4.
- **Your AirPods send 50 Hz on this Mac, not 25 Hz.** Using the full 50 Hz scored no better, so the app keeps 25 Hz because it's faster.

**Testing now happens throughout training:**
- **Test-then-train.** Before each take is saved, a model that has never seen the current block predicts it. The screen shows "Model heard: …" in green or red, and a live panel shows accuracy overall, per word, for the last 10 takes and by block.
- **Quiz rounds.** After each block there's a short quiz, one take per word, that is never used for training (on by default). There's also a standalone **Run quiz**. Evaluate shows the quiz score and can add quiz takes to training afterwards.

**You can change any setting:** the new **Tune** screen exposes the filter, sample rate, sensor channels, trimming, the recognizer settings, augmentation, and the recording window and lead-in. Changes re-score your existing takes immediately, with no re-recording. **Run auto-tune** tries about 60 combinations on your takes and ranks them. The same works from the terminal:

```bash
swift run -c release LouVoiceCheck --eval ~/Library/Application\ Support/LouVoice/dataset.json --tune
```

**Treat 68% with some caution.** You have about 9 takes per word, so one take moves a word's score by about 11 points, and picking the best of many settings flatters the result. The quiz score is the number to trust, because quiz takes are never trained or tuned on. The weakest spots are "can" (33%, mostly confused with "you") and "me" and "you" mixing with each other. Recording 2–3 more blocks is the biggest remaining lever.

The 9 core checks still pass, and the end-to-end smoke test on the simulator passes with the new testing and quiz steps. The decisions are logged as D29–D31 in [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md). ### D32: Self-normalising "too subtle" check; no calibration step (2026-11-07). *Supersedes the noise-floor part of D14.*
**Decision:** A take's **strength** is its smoothed peak activity divided by its own 20th-percentile activity. The "too subtle" rejections weren't your mouthing. The check compared every take against a resting noise level measured once, at the start of a session, and your saved level is **0.74**, ten times the 0.07 from your first session. That "stay still" step most likely caught some movement. Against the inflated level, **all 49** of your recorded words would have failed.

**The fix:**
- **Each take is measured against its own quiet part.** The recording window is about 2 seconds and a word fills about half a second, so the rest of the window gives a reliable baseline. A bad calibration can't block you any more.
- **The "Stay still" calibration step is gone** from enrollment, so sessions are a little shorter.
- **Rejections show the number**, e.g. "strength 2.4×, needs 3.0×", so you know how far off a take was.
- **The thresholds are adjustable:** Tune has a new Quality gate section where you can change the minimum strength and head-movement limits, or switch either check off.

**On your recorded takes:** your words range from 3.4× to about 20× strength, median 8.3×. The default minimum is 3×, so none of your 49 words would be rejected. Takes with no movement at all still are.

Using the word order is a strong idea, and it's exactly how speech recognisers work. The motion model gives a score for each word, and a **context model** says what's likely next: after "can", "you" is likely and "hello" isn't. Combining the two rules out the look-alike that doesn't fit the sentence.

                  let shuffled = Tuner.contextScore(rankings, phrase: words, context: c, chained: true, randomOrder: true) else { return }
            print(String(format: "%@  in order: words %3.0f%% phrase %3.0f%%   random order: words %3.0f%%",
                         name, inOrder.words * 100, inOrder.phrases * 100, shuffled.words * 100))
        }
        show("no context                       ", off)
        for w in [0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0] {
            for t in [0.05, 0.1, 0.2] {
                var c = ContextModel(); c.weight = w; c.temperature = t; c.smoothing = 0.1
                show(String(format: "weight %.2f temp %.2f smooth 0.10", w, t), c)
            }
        }
        exit(0)
    }

### D37: Next-word prediction from expected phrases; high-pass back to 0.8 Hz (2026-11-07)
**Data:** Session 4 (5 blocks with adaptive reps and drills, D36) brings the total to 356 takes: 280 training and 55 quiz in 12 blocks. Words rose to 63% and the quiz to 71% at the D33 settings.

**Motion defaults:** With 3× the data, **high-pass 0.8 Hz** is best. Words score **70%** and the quiz **42/55 (76%)**, against 63% and 71% at 1.2 Hz; 0.5 Hz and 1.0 Hz both score lower. The earlier moves to 1.2–1.6 Hz (D30, D33) came from too little data. Everything else stays as in D33 (rotation + attitude, magnitudes, 35% trim, k=3, ×8).

**Context model (the user's idea):** `ContextModel` is a smoothed bigram, P(word | previous), learned from a list of expected phrases (default "hello can you hear me"):
- After a phrase's last word, the next word is predicted like a phrase start.
- Motion scores become likelihoods, exp(−(score − best) / temperature), multiplied by the prior raised to a weight.
- Results are re-ranked as −log(posterior), so the existing margin rule still works.
- `_none` gets a neutral prior.
- The "too far" check uses the motion score before context.
- Context is the last kept word, and resets after 12 s idle or with "Restart phrase".

**Evaluation** (`LouVoiceCheck --context`): the phrase is simulated by drawing one held-out take per word from the same block. Each step's context is the previous **decoded** word (chained, so errors propagate). The same is repeated with **random word order**, to check that context doesn't override the motion.

| Preset (weight, temperature) | In order: words | In order: phrase | Random order: words |
|---|---|---|---|
| Off | 66% | 11% | 68% |
| **Balanced (0.3, 0.05)**, default | **75%** | 28% | 65% |
| Strong (0.5, 0.1) | 94% | 83% | 41% |
| Phrase lock (1.0, 0.1) | 100% | 99% | 24% |

**Why Balanced is the default:** a high weight looks perfect in order, but at Phrase lock it just recites the phrase, and out-of-order accuracy drops to about chance. Balanced gains 9 points in order for a 3-point cost out of order. Strong is a reasonable demo setting when the phrase is known; Phrase lock must not be presented as recognition.
**UI:** The Decode screen has a strength picker with these explanations, an editor for expected phrases, an "Expected next" line, and a note whenever context changed the motion's answer.
EOF

content.text:
Your idea works, and it's built into Decode. I tested it so it doesn't fool you.

**The new round helped a lot.** You added 5 blocks, 211 takes, with the adaptive reps and drills. Re-tuned on all 280 training takes, words went from 56% to **70%** and the quiz from 67% to **76%** (42/55). The bigger dataset showed the original 0.8 Hz filter is best after all; the earlier 1.2–1.6 Hz picks were based on too little data.

**How the prediction works:** the app learns which word tends to follow which from your expected phrases (default "hello can you hear me"). After "can", it strongly expects "you", so a take that looks halfway between "you" and "me" goes to "you". It uses its own previous answer as the context, so a wrong guess can mislead the next word, just as in real use.

**The catch:** set it too strong and it simply recites the phrase, whatever you mouth. So I also tested every setting with the words mouthed in **random order**:

| Strength | Phrase in order: words | Whole phrase right | Random order: words |
|---|---|---|---|
| Off | 66% | 11% | 68% |
| **Balanced** (default) | **75%** | 28% | 65% |
| **Strong** | **94%** | **83%** | 41% |
| Phrase lock | 100% | 99% | 24% (ignores your mouth) |

- **Balanced** is a clear win at almost no cost when you go off-script.
- **Strong** is a good demo setting for the known phrase: 94% of words right, and 83% of the time the whole sentence is right.
- **Phrase lock** is labelled as demo-only, because at that point it isn't really recognising anything.

**In the app (Decode screen):**
- **Next-word prediction:** pick the strength, with these trade-offs explained, and edit the expected phrases, one per line.
- **Expected next:** shows what it's predicting, e.g. "you 74% · …".
- **When context changes the answer,** it says so: "Motion alone said 'me'; the phrase context picked 'you'".
- **Restart phrase** clears the context. It also resets on its own after 12 seconds without a word.

LouVoice is rebuilt and reopened, and the reasoning is logged as D37. I haven't tried the prediction in the live app yet, only on your recorded takes, so check it on the Decode screen. Nothing is pushed to GitHub.

# LouVoice — instructions for Claude Code

LouVoice is a native macOS SwiftPM app that recognizes silently mouthed words from AirPods Pro 2 head-motion data and speaks them in the user's own ElevenLabs voice clone, for people with ALS.

**Source of truth:** the team's PRD. The original tech plan proved feasibility; where it conflicts with the PRD, the PRD wins. The current work order is `docs/PRD-CHANGES.md`.

## Rules

1. Work ONE checklist item from `docs/PRD-CHANGES.md` at a time, in order, starting with "Must do before the demo." Do not start the next item until the current one builds and `swift run LouVoiceCheck` (or `swift test`) passes.
2. Do not refactor or rewrite working code that an item doesn't require. M1–M4 currently work — keep them working.
3. Keep the one-word-per-trigger decode mode working at all times as a fallback, even while building continuous recognition.
4. Skip items that need a human (recording a session, creating accounts, creating the ElevenLabs voice). List them for the team instead.
5. Never hard-code API keys or commit them. Read the ElevenLabs key from the Keychain or an environment variable, and keep any key file in `.gitignore`.
6. When a choice isn't specified (thresholds, UI layout, schema fields), pick a sensible default, mark it with a `// TODO(team):` comment, and say what you chose.
7. After each item: summarize what changed, which files you touched, and how to test it by hand. Then stop and wait for "next."
8. Only change code and the tech plan document. Pitch and demo-script decisions belong to the team.

## Hard constraints (updated)

- Hardware: AirPods Pro 2 plus the Mac they're paired with.
- Word recognition uses head-motion data only. No webcam, no speech recognition.
- The microphone may be used only to record voice samples for the user's ElevenLabs voice clone, never for word recognition.
- Delivered as a native macOS app; data stays on the Mac by default. Anything sent to Tiger Data or a Vultr backend requires the user's explicit opt-in.
-----
# LouVoice: Tech Plan Changes to Match the PRD

The PRD is the source of truth now. The tech plan proved AirPods motion can tell words apart; these changes turn it into the product the PRD describes. Work top to bottom: the first section is what the Sunday demo needs.

## Must do before the demo

- [ ] **Add ElevenLabs voice output (new `VoiceService`).** The plan never speaks in the user's voice, and that's the core of the PRD. Use the user's ElevenLabs voice clone. Because the vocabulary is fixed, generate the audio for every word or phrase once at enrollment and cache it locally. Playback is then instant and doesn't depend on venue Wi-Fi. Fall back to live API calls only for words added since the last cache.
    - Keep the API key out of the app bundle: Keychain or an environment variable.
    - Done when: delay from the end of a mouthed word to the start of audio is under 1.5 s (PRD success test).
- [ ] **Recognize full sentences, not one word per button press.** The plan captures one fixed 1.8 s window per trigger. The PRD says the user mouths a full sentence. Stream motion continuously, detect where each word starts and stops (the energy trim in `Features.swift` is a starting point), and classify each segment as it ends. Keep the one-word-per-trigger mode as a demo fallback if continuous mode isn't reliable by Sunday.
    - Done when: "hello can you hear me" mouthed at a normal pace comes out as 5 words, in order, without pressing anything between them.
- [ ] **Hands-free start and stop.** The stem press, Space bar and nods all need finger or neck control, which people with ALS can lose. With continuous recognition, the app just listens. Add a simple on/off "listening" switch that a caregiver can control too.
- [ ] **Fast correction.** At today's 68% word accuracy, a 5-word sentence comes out fully right only about 15% of the time. Show the top 3 guesses under each word so one tap (by the user or caregiver) fixes it, and feed every confirmed or corrected word back into training. Nod/shake can stay as an option, not the only way.
- [ ] **Support phrases, not just single words.** Let a vocabulary entry be a phrase like "I love you" or "I'm tired." Enrollment and decoding need a longer capture limit for phrase entries.
- [ ] **Use the PRD's persona and vocabulary everywhere.** Alex Chen; demo phrase "hello can you hear me." The plan's demo section still says 8–10 words.
- [ ] **Voice banking during enrollment.** The tech plan bans the microphone, but the PRD doesn't, and Alex can still speak. While he can, have him say each word out loud during enrollment and record mic audio alongside the motion. That one session trains the motion model *and* collects clean samples for his ElevenLabs voice clone. The mic is used only to build the voice, never to recognize words. Test whether a model trained on spoken words still recognizes silently mouthed ones; if not, enroll both ways.
- [ ] **Voice clone setup in the app.** Add an onboarding step that creates the user's ElevenLabs voice: from enrollment audio if they can still speak, or from old recordings (videos, voicemails) if they can't. Link to the ElevenLabs Impact Program for free access.

## Should do before the demo

- [ ] **Re-check the 68% on a fresh session.** The settings were tuned on the same 59 takes they were scored on, so 68% may be optimistic. Record a new session, score it with the tuned settings, and put that number in the PRD and the pitch.
- [ ] **Try 50 Hz instead of 25 Hz.** The AirPods stream at 50 Hz, but the pipeline downsamples to 25 Hz. Change the resample rate, rerun the evaluation, and keep whichever scores higher.
- [ ] **Report the PRD's metrics.** Add sentence success rate and end-to-end delay (end of word to start of audio) to the Evaluate output, next to word accuracy.
- [ ] **Build a quick judge enrollment.** The PRD has a judge train the model. Add a short mode (3–5 words, 3 takes each, about 2 minutes) and show the judge their own accuracy honestly. Run the main demo on a teammate's fully trained model.
- [ ] **Make a user-facing dashboard.** Sensors and Evaluate are developer screens; hide them behind a developer toggle. The user sees the live transcript, the correction tap, and their voice playing back. Per the PRD: clean, cool, not like a medical device.

## Deterioration tracking and adaptation

The PRD's "Building for patient's needs" section commits to three things the plan doesn't have yet: enroll early, retrain word by word, and warn when the signal fades. For the demo, one working chart of a user's data over time is enough; the full loop can come after.

- [ ] **Tiger Data time-series.** After every session, log per word: movement strength (peak motion vs. the noise floor), accuracy on confirmed words, and speaking pace. Tiger Data stores it as a time series per user.
- [ ] **Vultr backend.** A small API on Vultr receives session metrics from the Mac app and writes them to Tiger Data; Vultr also hosts the landing page. Raw motion stays on the Mac unless the user opts in to uploading it.
- [ ] **Per-word retraining prompt.** When a word's accuracy over its last ~20 uses drops below a set threshold, prompt the user to retrain just that word (3 takes), not the whole vocabulary.
- [ ] **Recent takes count more.** Weight recent takes higher and retire old templates, so the model follows the user's current movements instead of how they moved months ago.
- [ ] **Allow for slower speech.** ALS slows speaking rate before it hurts clarity. Widen the time-warp augmentation (now ×0.85–1.15) and the DTW band so slower versions of a word still match.
- [ ] **Signal-fading alert.** When movement strength trends toward the noise floor, tell the user and caregiver that LouVoice is becoming unreliable, so they can plan another communication method in time.
- [ ] **Consent screen.** Explain what is uploaded, get explicit opt-in, and let the user delete their data. This is health data; it supports the PRD's dignity principle.

## Cut or change

- [ ] **Drop M7 from hackathon scope.** Xcode migration, Developer ID signing, notarized `.dmg`: none of it matters for judging. The ad-hoc build is enough.
- [ ] **Drop the live re-seat stunt.** Leave-one-block-out already re-seats the AirPods between every session, so that number proves re-seat robustness. Show the number instead of risking a live failure.
- [ ] **Don't claim GPU training for the current model.** The k-NN DTW recognizer trains on a laptop in seconds. Vultr GPUs only make sense if we move to a neural model later; say that, or describe Vultr as hosting the backend.
- [ ] **Rewrite M5–M6 around the PRD.** Replace them with: voice output, continuous sentence recognition, correction, deterioration tracking, then accuracy toward 90%.
- [ ] **Remove Solana** if it's referenced anywhere.

## Keep as is

- **The honest evaluation:** leave-one-block-out, the permutation test, the chance baseline, and labelling the optimistic number.
- **Re-seat correction, the `_none` rejection class and the quality checks on each take.**
- **Native macOS app with data stored locally by default.**

**What changed:**
- **Speaks in your cloned voice.** Every word Decode accepts is now spoken in your ElevenLabs voice clone instead of the system voice.
- **Each word is generated once and cached on the Mac**, so playback is instant and works without Wi-Fi. Generation runs after each enrollment, when you add a word, and at launch if anything is missing. A word that isn't cached yet is fetched live, then cached.

- **The delay is measured** from the end of the mouthed word to the start of audio. Decode shows it per word ("Voice 0.82 s after the word ended") plus the median and worst of the last 10, against the 1.5 s target.
- **Expected delay:** on your recorded takes, the word ends a median of 0.68 s before the capture window closes, so cached playback should come in around 0.7–0.9 s. Bluetooth adds about 0.1–0.2 s the app can't measure. The fixed window is now the main delay, and item 2 removes it.

**Files:**
- New: `Sources/LouVoice/VoiceService.swift`

- Also: `.gitignore`, and D39 in `DECISIONS.md`

**To test by hand:**
1. Create your voice clone in ElevenLabs. This step needs a person, so it's listed for the team below.
2. On **Decode**, open "Your voice (ElevenLabs)", paste your API key, and click **Save**.
3. Paste the **Voice ID** from your voice clone's page.
4. Click **Generate voice for all words**. It should show "Cached 5 of 5 words".
5. Click **Play test**. You should hear "hello" in your voice.
6. Decode a word. You should hear it in your voice, see the green delay line ("… · your voice (cached)"), and the median should stay under 1.5 s.
7. Turn Wi-Fi off and decode again. It should still speak, from the cache.

**Needs a person on the team:**
- Create an ElevenLabs account and API key.
- Create the voice clone from voice samples.

ok great what was the accuracy and lets rebuild to we achieve that 94, for the next training round lets train it on the sentance, and ill be speaking faster/flowing than usual

Here are the accuracy numbers from your latest data (280 training takes, settings now in the app):

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| Each word on its own (motion only, held-out blocks) | **70%** |
| Quiz takes | **76%** (42/55) |
| "hello can you hear me" in order, Strong next-word prediction | **94%** of words, whole phrase right **83%** of the time |

The rebuilt app already runs exactly this: 0.8 Hz filter plus Strong context, and no saved settings override it. **One caveat:** that 94% is for the phrase said **one word per beep**. Flowing, faster sentences are a different signal: words blur into each other and get shorter. Isolated-word templates won't match them well.

So training on the sentence needs real new machinery, which is the core of PRD item 2 (full sentences):

1. **Sentence decoding.** Press once, mouth the whole sentence. The app finds the word boundaries itself and uses the phrase context while doing it.
2. **Sentence training.** You mouth the full sentence flowing. Because the words are known, the app aligns them to the motion, cuts each one out, and adds those fast, joined-up versions as new word templates.

I'll build the core first, and test the boundary-finding on sentences stitched together from your existing word takes before you record anything.

### D40: Whole-sentence decoding and sentence training (2026-11-07). *PRD-CHANGES item 2, first part.*
**Decision:** A sentence mode where one press captures a 4 s window (`TODO(team)`: tune for longer phrases) and the whole sentence comes out word by word.
- `SentenceDecoder` runs a dynamic program over every way to split the motion into words. Each candidate segment is scored by DTW against that word's most recent 12 real templates (mean of the best 2), plus a per-word penalty and the next-word context (bigram).
- Speed: one open-ended DTW pass per (start frame, template) scores every possible end point at once. That's about 30× cheaper than one DTW per segment: **0.03 s per sentence**.
- The one-word-per-press mode stays as a fallback (Decode › Mode).

**Sentence training:** In Enroll, the user mouths the whole phrase, flowing, at their natural (fast) pace. Each take is:
1. decoded by a model that hasn't seen this block, giving an honest live score (words and whole sentence);
2. **forced-aligned** to the known words with the current model, cut into per-word sample windows (0.3 s lead-in, 0.15 s tail) and stored as ordinary word takes in a `sentence-…` block. This gives the recognizer fast, joined-up versions of each word;
3. stored whole as a sentence take (`Take.isSentence`, excluded from word training), so it can be re-cut later as the model improves.

Confirmed sentence decodes (nod or Y) are cut and learned the same way.

**Correction:** Each decoded word shows its 2 runner-up words as buttons; one tap replaces it. This is the start of PRD item 4.

**Tuning on stitched sentences** (`LouVoiceCheck --sentences [--grid]`): one held-out take per word, concatenated in phrase order, decoded by a model trained on the other blocks, at normal speed and 1.33× time-compressed. At Strong context:

| Per-word penalty / context weight | Normal: words | Normal: whole sentence | 1.33× faster: words | 1.33× faster: whole sentence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 / 4 (**chosen**) | 95% | 77% | 93% | 79% |
| 1.5 / 4 | 97% | 85% | 89% | 70% |
| 3 / 2 (first guess) | 88% | 71% | 82% | 50% |
| any / no context | 39–46% | 3–8% | 38–46% | 3–8% |

Penalty 0 was chosen because the user will speak faster. The context weight scales with the Decode strength (`SentenceConfig.contextWeight × context.weight`, so Strong = 4). Forced alignment puts word boundaries within about 0.1 s on average.

**Caveat:** Stitched sentences have no co-articulation. Real flowing sentences will score lower until sentence-training takes exist, which is what the next round collects.
**Not done yet (rest of item 2):** continuous listening with no press per sentence. That's planned together with item 3 (hands-free start and stop).

- **One press, the whole sentence.** Press once and mouth the full sentence in the 4 s window. The app finds the word boundaries itself, using your phrase as context. It takes about 0.03 s.
- **One tap to fix a word.** Under each decoded word are its two runner-ups as buttons, so you can correct a word without re-saying it.

|---|---|---|
| Normal | 95% | 77% |

**Sentence training, for your next round (Enroll › "Sentence training (flowing)"):**

2. Mouth the whole sentence after each beep, flowing, at your fast pace.

### D41: Full-history phrase model with end-of-sentence for sentence decoding (2026-11-07). *Amends D40.*
**Finding:** With the D40 bigram, every failed stitched sentence was the **wrong length**, never a wrong word. The two errors were:
- running on past the end, "hello can you hear me hello" (×19), caused by the word-mode rule that wraps the last word back to the first;
- stopping early, "hello can you" (×18 at the faster pace), because ending a sentence cost nothing.

**Decision:** Sentence decoding uses a **prefix tree of the expected phrases** (`PhraseTrie`) instead of the bigram:
- P(next word) depends on the whole history said so far.
- Each phrase has an explicit **end-of-sentence** mark, so stopping early or running on is penalised.
- An unexpected word leaves the tree (via smoothing) into a "free" state, where every word and ending are equally likely.
- The decoder's dynamic-program state is the tree node.
- Word mode keeps the bigram with wrap-around, which is right between separate presses.

**Results** (stitched held-out takes; words / whole sentence right; per-word penalty 0):

| Test | Off | Balanced | Strong |
|---|---|---|---|
| "hello can you hear me", normal | 30% / 2% | 98% / 95% | 99% / 96% |
| … 1.33× faster | 31% / 1% | 100% / 100% | 100% / 100% |
| 4 known phrases, say any | 30% / 9% | 87% / 82% | 88% / 83% |
| Off-script random 3–5 words | 37% / 7% | 26% / 2% | 20% / 0% |

Penalties of 1 and 2 changed nothing material.

**What this means (for honest claims):**
- With a single known phrase, near-100% is guaranteed by the prior and proves little.
- The real evidence is **choosing among several known phrases from motion: 83% whole-phrase right**, against 9% without context.
- Context makes LouVoice a **phrasebook**: off-script sentences get worse, because they're pulled towards known phrases.
- For the demo, register several phrases so the choice is real. The PRD already scopes LouVoice to trained words and phrases.
- Stitched sentences lack co-articulation, so real flowing sentences need confirming with the sentence-training round.

content.text:
You were right: word order should make it nearly certain, and the gap was a flaw in my context model.

**What was going wrong:** every failed sentence was the **wrong length**, never a wrong word.
- **Running on.** "hello can you hear me **hello**" (×19). I'd let the model treat "me" as leading back to "hello", which is right between separate presses, but wrong inside one sentence.
- **Stopping early.** "hello can you" (×18 at fast pace). The model only looked at the previous word and had no idea where a sentence ends.

**The fix is your idea, done properly:** a phrase model that knows **everything said so far**. After "hello can you" it predicts "hear"; after "…hear me" it predicts **end of sentence**. With several phrases, it tells them apart by the whole history.

| Pace | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | 80% whole sentence | **96%** (99% of words) |
| 33% faster | 73% | **100%** |

**The part to be careful with in the pitch:** with one known phrase, 100% proves little, because the model can recite it without reading your mouth. So I tested two harder cases:
- **4 known phrases, say any one** ("hello", "can you hear me", "hear me", "hello can you hear me"): it picks the right phrase **83%** of the time from motion, against 9% without context. That's the real evidence LouVoice reads the motion.
- **Off-script random words:** context makes these worse, 20% of words against 37% with context off, because it pulls everything towards a known phrase. LouVoice behaves like a **phrasebook**, which fits the PRD's "only knows trained words and phrases".

**For the demo,** add a few phrases in Decode › Next-word prediction › Expected phrases, so the choice is genuine. These are all stitched from your word takes; your sentence-training round will show how real flowing speech compares.

Do you think we can use synthetic data to better train other sentances aswell at this point, you dont need to say yes only if confident

No, not for training. I'm not confident it would help, for three reasons:

- **New sentences from words you've already trained need no extra data.** The sentence decoder matches each word against your recorded takes, and the phrase model only needs the *text*. Type "can you hear me" or "hear me hello" into Expected phrases and it works immediately. Stitched synthetic sentences would just recycle the same word takes, so the model learns nothing new.
- **Sentences with new words ("I love you", "I'm tired") can't be synthesised credibly.** The motion signature of a word you've never mouthed can't be invented from the AirPods signal. My simulator's word signatures are made up, and articulography datasets record mouth movement with sensors placed on the tongue and jaw, not at the ear, with no reliable mapping to it. Training on that would teach the model fiction.
- **Fast, joined-up speech is better learned from the real thing.** Squeezing and blending word takes is roughly what the time-warp augmentation already does. The forced-aligned word cuts from your sentence-training round are genuinely joined-up takes, which is much better data.

Where synthetic data *is* worth it, and I am confident here, is **choosing phrases before you record them.** The stitched-sentence test I just ran can score any set of phrases built from trained words. It shows whether they're distinct enough from each other ("hear me" vs "hello"), and whether a set is too confusable to trust in the demo. That's how I got the 83% for picking among 4 phrases.

So for other sentences:
- **Same five words:** just add the phrases as text. I can score a candidate list for you first.
- **New words:** record them with the usual blocks, then one sentence-training round for the phrases they appear in.
- **When choosing new phrases:** prefer ones that differ in length and syllable rhythm, because that's what the sensor sees best.
great now lets think how can we make it more durable vs subtle head movements or moving

Here's what we have today, why moving still hurts, and what I'd do, with how confident I am in each.

**What's already protecting you:**
- **The 0.8 Hz filter** strips out slow posture drift and slow turns.
- **The re-seat correction** cancels how the earbud sits and how the head is tilted.
- **The accelerometer is already dropped.** Rotation and head-angle data only, which happens to remove most walking bounce.
- **The quality check** rejects training takes where the head turned more than 15°.
- **The "not a word" class** absorbs pure head movements like turns and nods.

**Why moving still hurts:** quick head movements (small nods, glances, turns at about 1–3 Hz) fall in the same frequency range as jaw movement, so no filter can separate them. Without a second sensor, there's no clean "head only" reference. MuteIt used a second IMU for exactly this; we can't, because the Mac only receives one fused stream and won't say which earbud it came from.

**What I'd do, in order:**

1. **Measure first (confident).** Mix *real* head motion from your recorded turns, nods and look-ups into held-out word takes at increasing strength, and see how fast accuracy falls. That's legitimate synthetic use, because it's your own recorded motion added to your own recorded words, and it's only used for testing. Without this we'd be guessing which fix helps.
2. **Record "while moving" blocks (most confident).** One or two training blocks where you mouth while naturally moving: small nods, glances, shifting in the chair, maybe walking. Real examples of words-with-movement are what a template matcher needs. The adaptive reps and the test-then-train score would show immediately whether it helps.
3. **Movement masking (fairly confident).** Detect frames where head rotation is clearly bigger than any jaw movement in your data, and down-weight them in the matching instead of letting them dominate. In sentence mode, the decoder could treat a movement burst as a pause instead of forcing it into a word.
4. **Head-motion augmentation in training (moderately confident).** Add your recorded head movements onto training takes as extra copies. It teaches tolerance, but it can also blur the templates, so I'd only keep it if step 1 shows a gain.
5. **"Hold still" feedback in decode (confident it's useful UX).** If a capture had a big head movement, say so ("Head moved, try again") instead of outputting a wrong word. Fewer wrong words beats more attempted words.

I'd **skip** subtracting head motion with clever filters (it overlaps the jaw band, so it removes words too) and using the iPhone as a reference sensor (extra hardware).

My recommendation: I build the measurement (step 1) plus masking (step 3) and hold-still feedback (step 5) now. You record one "while moving" block next round (step 2), and the measurement then tells us whether augmentation (step 4) is worth adding.

Yes. Here's the plan:
1. **Build a robustness test.** Mix your real recorded head movements (the turns, nods, chewing and look-ups in your "not a word" takes) into held-out word takes at increasing strength, and see how fast accuracy falls.
2. **Try fixes against it:**
   - **Noisy training copies:** add head motion onto training takes.
   - **Soft clipping:** big head-motion spikes can't dominate the match.
   - **A head-movement gate:** say "head moved" rather than guess.
3. **Keep only what measurably helps,** on clean takes as well as noisy ones.

### D42: Train with recorded movement mixed in; soft-clip features (2026-11-07)
**Test method** (`LouVoiceCheck --eval … --robust`):
- Take each held-out word, then mix in the movement from a real recorded "not a word" take (turn, nod, look up, chew, swallow, smile) from *another* block, at 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0× its recorded strength. `Interference.mix` adds rotation rate and acceleration, and composes the extra rotation onto the attitude and gravity.
- The model trains on the other blocks, as in leave-one-block-out.

**Finding:** Movement is very damaging. A quarter-strength head movement drops word accuracy from 69% to 38%.

| Variant | 0 | 0.25 | 0.5 | 1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 69% | 38% | 26% | 11% |
| Soft clip 3σ only | 69% | 37% | 22% | 12% |
| Noisy training ×2 | 68% | 45% | 41% | 20% |
| **Noisy ×2 + soft clip 3σ (chosen)** | **68%** | **45%** | **42%** | **25%** |
| Noisy ×6 (0.2–1.0×) + clip | 68% | 47% | 42% | 31% |
| Head gate 10° (no noise training) | 69% | 49%, answers 55% | 38%, answers 53% | 27%, answers 42% |

Each cell uses one random movement per test take, so it carries about ±3 points of noise.

**Decision:**
- **2 noisy training copies per word take** (`RobustnessConfig.noiseCopies`): random recorded movement at 0.3–0.8× strength, time-shifted ±0.3 s.
- **Soft clipping at 3σ** (`ClassifierConfig.softClip`), so one big spike can't dominate a DTW distance.
- About +7 to +17 points under movement, for about 1 point on clean takes.
- ×6 was only slightly better and makes matching 3× heavier, so it isn't the default.

**Details:**
- Noisy copies are marked synthetic and never used as sentence templates, so sentence decoding still matches against real takes. Clean stitched sentences are unchanged: 95% / 100% whole sentence.
- Building the noisy set runs off the main thread (about 1 s per retrain).
- **"Hold still" gate:** decode can refuse a capture whose head turned more than N° ("Head moved 23°, hold still and try again"). It's off by default, since the gate trades answers for accuracy; it's on Tune › Robustness.

**Limits:**
- This uses mixed recordings, not real "mouthing while moving" takes, and it doesn't cover walking.
- The strongest next step is a training block recorded while moving naturally, which these numbers can then be checked against.
- The app's Evaluate screen still measures clean leave-one-block-out without noisy copies; `--robust` is the movement benchmark.
EOF

content.text:
Yes. I added noise to the training data, measured it on your takes, and kept what helped.

**How I tested it:** I took your real recorded movements (the turns, nods, look-ups, chewing and swallowing in your "not a word" takes) and mixed them into held-out word takes at increasing strength. These are takes from a block the model never trained on, so this is a realistic "mouthing while moving" test built from real recordings.

**What it showed:** movement does a lot of damage. Even a quarter-strength head movement dropped word accuracy from 69% to 38%.

| Movement mixed in | None | 25% | 50% | Full |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Before | 69% | 38% | 26% | 11% |
| **Now** (noisy training + soft clipping) | **68%** | **45%** | **42%** | **25%** |

**What's now in the app (on by default):**
- **Noisy training copies:** each word take gets 2 extra copies with a random recorded movement mixed in, so words are learned with motion on top.
- **Soft clipping:** one big head-motion spike can no longer dominate the match.
- **Sentences still match against real takes,** never the noisy copies. Clean sentences are unchanged: 95% at normal pace and 100% when faster.
- **The extra training runs in the background**, about a second per retrain, so enrollment doesn't stutter.
- **An optional "hold still" check** on Tune › Robustness (off by default): Decode can refuse a capture where your head turned more than a set angle, with "Head moved 23°, hold still and try again". It trades fewer answers for fewer wrong ones.

**What I didn't try:**
- **More copies (×6)** helped only slightly and makes matching 3× heavier.
- **Soft clipping alone** didn't help.

**Still the biggest lever:** a training block recorded *while* you move naturally (small nods, glancing, shifting, maybe walking). These numbers come from mixed recordings, not real mouthing-while-moving, and walking isn't covered. Once you've recorded one, I can check whether the measured gains hold up.

The app is rebuilt and reopened, the checks pass, and the reasoning is logged as D42. Nothing is committed.

content.text:
Fixed, and LouVoice is reopened, ready for sentence training. There were two causes.

**1. Dropped words (the main one):**
- **Cause:** your trained word takes are long, about 0.7–0.9 s each, because isolated words are mouthed slowly. The sentence decoder wouldn't squeeze a word into less than half that, about 0.3 s, but in fast, flowing speech words are shorter. Words that didn't fit got merged or dropped.
- **Reproduced:** on sentences stitched from your takes and sped up, whole sentences fell from 97% to **49% at 2.5× speed** and **8% at 3×**.
- **Fix:** words can now be squeezed to a quarter of their trained length. Results are **100% up to 3× faster**, and telling several phrases apart is no worse.

**2. Clipped endings:**
- The window used to stop at a fixed 4 s. It now **ends when you stop mouthing**: 0.8 s after your last movement, never before 1 s after the beep, and up to 6 s if you need it.
- I replayed that rule over your 314 recorded word takes. It **never cut off a word mid-way**.
- Faster speech also means the voice comes back sooner.

**Things to know before you train:**
- **There's no ElevenLabs key set,** so the voice you hear is the Mac's built-in voice.
- **If it cuts you off during a natural pause,** raise "…after stillness of" (Tune › Sentence, now 0.8 s). The fastest-word limit is adjustable there too.

**Start sentence training:** Enroll › **Sentence training (flowing)** › **Start sentence training**, default 5 sentences × 3 blocks.
- **Mouth the whole sentence after the beep,** at your fast natural pace, then hold still.
- **The live panel** shows how often the whole sentence comes out right, per block.
- **Each sentence is cut into its words and learned,** so the templates catch up with your real fast pace. That makes the squash fix matter less over time.

Varied-length sentence training is built and LouVoice is reopened. Decoding parts reliably isn't solved yet, though; details below.

**Sentence training now varies the length.** With "Vary the length" on (the default), each take prompts either the full "hello can you hear me" (about 40% of takes) or a random part like "hello can", "can you hear" or "you hear me".
- **The recording limit scales** with how many words are prompted.
- **The live score** allows for parts.
- **Each take is cut into the words it actually contained,** so every part becomes correct word training data.

**Decoding parts is the hard bit, measured on sentences stitched from your takes:**
- **With the decoder expecting the full phrase only** (the default), the full phrase stays at **97–100%**, but parts come out right only **7–8%** of the time, because it pushes them towards the full sentence.
- **Telling it to also expect parts** lifts parts to **about 38%**, but fast full sentences drop sharply.
- **The cause:** your word templates come from slow isolated words, so the decoder has to squash them a lot. At that point "can you" at normal pace and "can you hear me" at double pace fit the motion equally well, so motion can't tell how many words you said.
- **I tried a pace model** (one steady pace per sentence). Even when I gave it the true pace, parts only reached **35–39%** whole-sentence right.

**Where things stand:**
- **Decoding stays on whole phrases by default,** so the demo sentence stays reliable.
- **There's a switch** on Decode, "Also expect parts", with the trade-off shown.
- **Your varied-length round is the real fix.** It gives fast templates that don't need heavy squashing, real phrase starts and ends, and your actual pace.

**To record it:** Enroll › **Sentence training (flowing)**, with "Vary the length" ticked, then **Start sentence training**. Mouth whatever words appear, flowing, then hold still. Afterwards I'll re-measure parts on your real sentences and tune them, before suggesting turning parts on.

### D46: Two votes for the demo sentence choice: word alignment + whole-sentence matching (2026-11-07). *Extends D45.*
**Data:** 754 takes:

**Decision:** Demo mode combines two independent votes:
- (a) the total cost of aligning the motion to each phrase word by word;
- (b) DTW of the **whole sentence** against the user's recorded sentences of each phrase (mean of the 3 nearest).

Each vote is a log-ratio against the candidates' mean, summed with weight 1. If any candidate phrase has no recorded sentences, alignment is used alone.
- The references are rebuilt off the main thread with each retrain (`AppModel.sentenceReferences`).
- In sentence training, the live honest score uses references from **other** blocks only.

**Caveat:** 45 takes is a small sample, and 100% on it isn't a guarantee. The thinnest correct margin was 0.05. Every extra mixed-sentence block makes vote (b) stronger, and it can be re-checked with `--demo`.

### D47: Demo mode says "no sentence" for random movement (2026-11-07)
**Request:** Sentence decoding must recognise when no sentence was said, for example random movement.

**Test** (`LouVoiceCheck --reject`; every block held out):
- **Positives:** the 45 real demo-sentence takes.
- **Negatives:** 54 recorded movement takes (chew, swallow, turn, nod, smile, look up) and 593 single-word takes, since a lone word isn't one of the demo sentences either.

**Scores per capture:**
- (a) word-by-word alignment cost per frame for the chosen phrase;
- (b) distance to the nearest recorded demo sentences ÷ distance to the nearest "nothing" references (movement takes plus 120 single words).

Combined score = ln(a ÷ 0.5) + ln(b); higher means less sentence-like.

**Finding:** Requiring every real sentence to be kept forces thresholds so loose that 8–22 of the 54 movements get through. The combined score gives a clean trade-off:

| Threshold | Sentences kept | Movement accepted | Single words accepted |
|---|---|---|---|
| < 0.2 | 39/45 | 0/54 | 8/593 |
| **< 0.6 (chosen)** | **42/45** | **0/54** | **45/593** |
| < 0.7 | 43/45 | 3/54 | 62/593 |
| < 1.0 | 43/45 | 11/54 | 127/593 |

Adding single words to the "nothing" references cut wrongly accepted single words roughly in half compared with movement-only references.

**Decision:** Demo mode rejects at score ≥ 0.6 (`SentenceConfig.rejectThreshold`; `TODO(team)`). It shows "No sentence detected — looked like other movement" and plays the reject tone instead of speaking. A strictness slider and an on/off switch are on Decode. The references are rebuilt with each retrain. The live sentence-training score never rejects.

**Trade-off accepted:** About 1 in 15 real sentences is refused ("try again"), in exchange for never speaking a sentence in response to random movement. More mixed-sentence blocks should tighten real sentences' scores and lower that refusal rate.

The two sentences are now told apart perfectly on your real takes, and random movement gets "no sentence" instead of a guess. LouVoice is reopened with both changes.

**Your data:** you recorded the 7 new words (about 21–25 takes each) and **45 real sentences**: 29 × "hello can you hear me" and 16 × "my name is konrad how are you today". With 12 words, isolated-word accuracy is 50%; "today", "are" and "konrad" are still thin. That doesn't matter much for the demo, because sentences are judged as a whole.

**Telling the two sentences apart:** each test sentence was scored by a model that never saw its block.

| Method | Right |
|---|---|
| Word-by-word alignment alone | 44/45 |
| Matching against your recorded whole sentences alone | 44/45 |
| **Both combined (now in demo mode)** | **45/45** |

The two methods each got a *different* take wrong, which is why combining them fixed both. 45 takes is still a small sample, so the closest call matters: it won by a margin of 0.05, against a typical 0.54.

**"No sentence" for random movement (new):** I tested against your 54 recorded movements (chewing, swallowing, turns, nods, smiles) and 593 single words, which also aren't one of the demo sentences.

| | Result at the chosen setting |
|---|---|
| Random movement accepted as a sentence | **0 of 54** |
| Real sentences kept | 42 of 45; 3 get "No sentence detected, try again" |
| Single words accepted as a sentence | 45 of 593 (8%) |

Making it accept every real sentence would have let a quarter of random movements through. Refusing 1 in 15 real sentences, so you just say it again, is much safer for a demo than speaking a sentence nobody said. The strictness slider on Decode shifts this trade-off.

**To make it tighter:** another round or two of mixed sentence training adds more references to match against, which should lower the refusal rate. `swift run -c release LouVoiceCheck --eval <dataset> --demo` re-checks the two-sentence choice after each round, and `--reject` the "no sentence" trade-off.

The checks pass, and this is logged as D46 and D47. Nothing is committed yet.
